newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn to miss EMU debt target - German magazine.
newsitem.headline: Bonn to miss EMU debt target - German magazine.

text.p: Finance Ministry experts have calculated Germany will miss the Maastricht national debt target necessary to qualify for European monetary union (EMU), a news magazine reported on Saturday.

Focus magazine said the experts had predicted Germany's debt would rise from 60.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996 to 61.5 percent this year. The Maastricht Treaty stipluates a maximum figure of 60 percent.
The weekly magazine, in an advance release from its Monday edition, did not name the experts or indicate their seniority and did not say where or how it had obtained their forecast.
A Finance Ministry spokeswoman said it was too early to make any prediction on Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio, adding Bonn was committed to doing everything possible to meet the Maastricht targets.

She said the ministry had made no official prediction like the one reported by Focus, although she could not rule out the possibility that the magazine had spoken to some if its officials independently.

Focus said that although the Maastricht Treaty makes provision for countries which miss the debt target to take part in EMU if they are deemed to be reducing their debt sufficiently, Germany's debt had been climbing since 1991.

It suggested privatisation proceeds could come to Germany's rescue. The magazine said such income could not be used to meet the Maastricht criteria for budget deficits but could be used for the debt target.
The ministry earlier denied a report that Bonn wanted payments to the European Union to be taken into account when the bloc decides which countries have met the deficit target.

The daily newspaper Bild quoted Finance Minister Theo Waigel as telling the parliamentary budget committee: "When it comes to meeting the Maastricht criteria, then crediting German payments to the EU must also be discussed."

It said this meant Germany's net contribution to EU coffers of 21 billion marks ($12.4 billion) a year could be subtracted from Bonn's budget deficit, ensuring it was inside the three percent of GDP to qualify for the single currency.
A ministry spokeswoman said the report was wrong, adding that Waigel had merely pointed out to the committee the heavy burden placed on Germany through its big payments to the EU.
"We're not pulling any tricks," the spokeswoman said.
German officials have been staunch advocates of a strict application of the Maastricht criteria for monetary union, insisting no creative accounting be used to meet the targets.
EU members are scheduled to decide in early 1998 which countries will be in the first wave of monetary union, which is due to begin in 1999. Their decision will be based on financial data for 1997.
